issues.legal_issue: A customary right to use irrigation water without charge continues after proprietary rights in the land and water source vest in the State.
material_facts: The holders of agricultural land had used water from the reservoir for irrigation without charge over generations before vesting, subject to maintaining the tank and channels.
The customary right to free irrigation was recorded in the village record of rights.
The applicable abolition legislation preserved tenants’ existing rights and recognized customary irrigation rights of tenants and malik-makbuza holders.
issues.conclusion: The customary right to free irrigation continued after vesting and could not be curtailed by the State.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 45(1), 46 and 47 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 preserved tenants’ existing rights, extended relevant customary rights to malik-makbuza holders, and required customs concerning irrigation to be ascertained and recorded. The Court also referred to Harrop v. Hirst for the proposition that water rights may be acquired by custom.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_ruling and right_exercised_before_vesting and customary_free_irrigation and right_recorded_in_village_record

predicates.appeal_from_writ_ruling: The matter is an appeal from a ruling on a petition challenging government action.
predicates.right_exercised_before_vesting: Landholders used the water for irrigation before the relevant property vested in the State.
predicates.customary_free_irrigation: Landholders had a customary practice of using the water for irrigation without charge.
predicates.right_recorded_in_village_record: The customary irrigation arrangement was recorded in the village record of rights.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a ruling on a petition challenging government action concerns a recorded customary practice of free irrigation exercised before vesting, the customary irrigation right continues after vesting.

issues.legal_issue: A right acquired under repealed legislation survives when the succeeding legislation preserves rights acquired under the repealed enactments.
material_facts: The right to free irrigation had accrued under provisions of the abolition legislation.
The Land Revenue Code repealed those provisions but included a clause preserving rights acquired under repealed enactments.
The State argued that repeal extinguished the right, while the landholders relied on the saving clause.
issues.conclusion: The repeal did not extinguish the acquired right to free irrigation; the right remained protected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 238 and 239 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954 repealed earlier provisions and preserved, so far as possible, rights acquired under the repealed enactments. Applying State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, the Court held that the question is whether the succeeding law manifests an intention to destroy the former rights, not merely whether it expressly keeps them alive.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_ruling: The matter is an appeal from a ruling on a petition challenging government action.
predicates.right_acquired_under_repealed_law: A person acquired a right under a law that was later repealed.
predicates.later_law_preserves_acquired_rights: The succeeding law preserves rights acquired under the enactments it repeals.

issues.definition: If an appeal from a ruling on a petition challenging government action concerns a right acquired under repealed legislation and the succeeding law preserves acquired rights, the acquired right survives repeal.

issues.legal_issue: The State cannot use its statutory authority over natural water bodies to charge for water taken from an artificial tank in a way that interferes with an existing customary irrigation right.
material_facts: The State demanded charges for irrigation water and required the landholders to agree in writing to pay them.
The water source was a tank constructed by people, not a natural lake or other natural collection of water.
The landholders had an established customary right to use the water for irrigation without charge.
issues.conclusion: The State was not competent under the asserted statutory authority to levy the charges or interfere with the customary right.
issues.legal_principle: Section 26 of the Central Provinces Irrigation Act, 1931 vests in the Government rights in water of specified natural sources, including rivers, natural streams, natural drainage channels, natural lakes and other natural collections of water. The Court held that the provision did not apply to the artificial tank and that the established customary right could not be interfered with. It referred to Harrop v. Hirst concerning the acquisition of water rights by custom and to Allen v. Petrick concerning the importance of irrigation use.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_ruling and state_sought_irrigation_charges and water_source_is_artificial and customary_free_irrigation

predicates.appeal_from_writ_ruling: The matter is an appeal from a ruling on a petition challenging government action.
predicates.state_sought_irrigation_charges: The State demanded payment for water used for irrigation.
predicates.water_source_is_artificial: The water source was constructed by people rather than being a natural water body.
predicates.customary_free_irrigation: Landholders had a customary practice of using the water for irrigation without charge.

issues.definition: When the State seeks irrigation charges for water from an artificial source already used under a customary practice of free irrigation, it cannot charge for or displace that customary use.
